name: Camera lens distortion (portrait lens 85mm)

card.summary: Using a longer lens from farther back to reduce nose and face distortion; the optics are well documented.

quick.overview:
Wide-angle lenses used up close enlarge features nearest the camera, such as the nose. Longer lenses, often cited as 85-135 mm, used from farther away flatten the effect.

The optics are described in photography references. No study has tested how this changes rated attractiveness.
quick.mechanism: Perspective is set mainly by camera-to-subject distance. A longer lens lets the photographer stand farther back while still framing the face, reducing relative size differences between facial features.

lead: Choosing a longer portrait lens, around 85 mm and up on a full-frame camera, and shooting from a greater distance is a photography technique used to make a face look more balanced in pictures. Perspective distortion makes features nearest the lens look larger: a face photographed up close with a wide-angle lens makes the nose appear bigger relative to the rest of the face, while a telephoto lens used from farther away makes it appear smaller.[1]

Portrait photography references name roughly 85-135 mm (35 mm equivalent) as a good range for portraits, with 75-135 mm cited for head-and-shoulders shots, and note that very short lenses exaggerate the nose and shrink the ears.[1][2] People who care about how they look in photos, profile pictures and dating app images use this to get a face that looks closer to how others see it in person.

A 2018 study in JAMA Facial Plastic Surgery by Ward and colleagues examined nasal distortion in short-distance photographs, the so-called selfie effect, and a follow-up exchange in the same journal discussed whether perceived distortions in selfies reflect viewing habits.[3][4]

chain: Longer lens and greater camera distance
Less perspective exaggeration of nose and central features
Face looks more balanced in photos
angle.text: Perspective in a photograph depends mainly on distance from the subject, so shooting from farther away with a longer lens reduces the enlargement of the nose and central face. This changes how the face appears in pictures without changing the face.

infobox: Portraits, profile photos, selfies versus rear camera shots

paras: Linear perspective is determined mainly by the camera's distance from the subject rather than by the lens itself; two shots from the same position have the same perspective geometry.[1] Wide-angle lenses are normally used close, and telephoto lenses from farther away, so lens choice and distance usually go together.[1]

Viewing distance also matters: viewing a wide-angle image from closer, or a telephoto image from farther away, reduces apparent distortion.[1] Extremely long lenses can flatten facial features excessively.[1]

Portrait references describe moderate telephoto focal lengths as the traditional choice for flattering head-and-shoulders portraits, because they allow a comfortable distance and render facial proportions more evenly.[2] Phone selfie cameras, held at arm's length with wide fields of view, sit at the short-distance end of the range described in the literature on the selfie effect.[3]

A 2018 JAMA Facial Plastic Surgery study examined how short-distance photographs distort the apparent size of the nose, the selfie effect.[3] A subsequent letter exchange discussed whether perceived selfie distortions are explained by viewing habits.[4] No studies of lens choice as a looksmaxxing practice were found.

timeline.event: Ward, Ward, Fried and Paskhover publish a study of nasal distortion in short-distance photographs in JAMA Facial Plastic Surgery.[3]
